question: Does recursively replacing scalar activations with shared lower-height ReLU subnetworks yield better function-approximation rates per distinct trainable parameter than ordinary width-and-depth ReLU networks?

key_findings.claim: A height-s NestNet recursively uses lower-height scalar networks as shared activation functions and counts each distinct activation subnetwork only once in its parameter budget.
key_findings.evidence: Height zero contains identity and ReLU; height one is an ordinary network; at greater height, activation-vector entries are functions realized by lower-height NestNets. The definition sums affine-map parameters and parameters of the distinct activation-function set, regardless of how many neurons reuse each activation.

key_findings.claim: The main theorem gives a constructive approximation rate governed by height and the target's modulus of continuity.
key_findings.evidence: For continuous f on the d-dimensional unit cube, Theorem 2.1 constructs a height-s NestNet with C(s,d)(n+1) distinct parameters and Lp error at most 7 square-root-d times omega_f of n raised to -(s+1)/d. For alpha-Hölder f, this becomes 7 lambda square-root-d times n raised to -(s+1)alpha/d.

key_findings.claim: The proof obtains its rate by using nested composition to implement fine quantization and encode many sampled target values in a small set of reused real parameters.
key_findings.evidence: The construction partitions the domain into K^d cells with K on the order of n^((s+1)/d), maps each cell to an integer index using almost-step functions, and decodes approximations to f at cell representatives. Appendix bit-extraction and lookup lemmas implement the large table through nested functions.

key_findings.claim: The theoretical advantage is a distinct-parameter result, not an advantage at matched computation graph size, FLOPs, memory traffic, numerical precision, or latency.
key_findings.evidence: The authors explicitly state that every NestNet can be expanded into a sufficiently large ordinary network and that the improvement comes from repeated reuse of activation-subnetwork parameters. Expansion counts the same activation weights many times and exposes potentially much larger executed structure that is absent from the stated parameter complexity.

key_findings.claim: The phrase 'overcome the curse of dimensionality' is qualified by height, hidden execution cost, constants, and unrestricted real-number encoding.
key_findings.evidence: The exponent reaches at least one only after choosing s+1 at least d; the uniform-norm constant includes 10^(d+3), and the proof stores and extracts increasingly many bits from real-valued parameters with no weight-magnitude or precision budget. The paper does not bound expanded units, arithmetic operations, numerical conditioning, or bit complexity.

key_findings.claim: A shared learned activation produces very large gains on a deliberately oscillatory spiral classification task, with substantial extra runtime.
key_findings.evidence: Adding one ten-parameter width-three activation subnetwork raises test accuracy from 0.738290 to 0.873631 at width 20, 0.816048 to 0.995962 at width 35, and 0.866118 to 0.999984 at width 50. Training time rises from 2,532 to 4,016 seconds, 2,595 to 4,104 seconds, and 2,642 to 4,218 seconds respectively.

key_findings.claim: The only standard image benchmark shows a small absolute accuracy gain that is not evaluated for significance or matched compute.
key_findings.evidence: On Fashion-MNIST, average last-100-epoch accuracy rises from 0.924447 to 0.926032 and the best accuracy from 0.925290 to 0.926620, while training time rises from about 5,802 to 7,217 seconds. Results are a symmetric trimmed mean after discarding the best and worst three of 18 trials, but no interval or paired test is given.

key_findings.claim: The experiments do not directly validate the theorem's rate or isolate height from a trainable-activation and optimization advantage.
key_findings.evidence: Both experiments use only height two and a hand-initialized ten-parameter activation with a learning rate five times smaller than other weights. There is no approximation-error scaling sweep, arbitrary-function regression, expanded weight-tied baseline, equal-FLOP deeper network, generic trainable-activation baseline, or ablation of activation initialization.

key_findings.claim: The implemented height-two activation is algebraically an existing variable-activation-function design, so the practical mechanism is not itself new.
key_findings.evidence: The experiment uses rho(x)=w1-transpose ReLU(x w0+b0)+b1 with three hidden hinges and ten parameters. Apicella et al.'s 2019 VAF already defines a learned weighted sum of shifted/scaled base activations, uses k=3 ReLU units, supports parameter sharing and ordinary backpropagation, and evaluates CNNs including Fashion-MNIST. The target cites the authors' later survey but does not compare this direct antecedent.

method.core_idea: Make a scalar activation itself a recursively defined trainable ReLU network and share it across many neurons, adding height as a measure of nesting depth.
method.mechanism: Define height recursively, count each distinct scalar activation subnetwork once, and construct quantizer/indexer/lookup modules that reuse these subnetworks to represent a very large piecewise approximation with few distinct weights. In experiments, replace selected ReLUs with one shared width-three, one-hidden-layer activation subnetwork initialized to a specified piecewise-linear function.
assumptions: Distinct trainable-parameter count is the relevant resource even when parameters are executed many times.
Real-valued parameters can store arbitrarily fine target-dependent information without a precision or magnitude charge.
Existence of a constructive approximant reflects a learnable architecture despite non-smooth lookup constructions.
The standard-network comparison does not grant an equivalent weight-sharing computation budget.
Hölder regularity and approximation norm capture the target tasks of interest.
A single shared activation and special optimizer schedule are representative of higher NestNet heights.

techniques.role: Turns lower-height scalar ReLU networks into reusable activations at the next height.
Charges a shared activation subnetwork once regardless of its number of call sites.
Maps fine domain cells to discrete indices outside small transition regions.
Decodes many table entries from compact real-valued encodings.
Repairs the approximation across narrow boundaries to obtain full-domain bounds.
Implements the height-two proof-of-concept used in classification.

evaluations.setting: Two interleaved 30-turn Archimedean spiral tubes; 600,000 train and 60,000 test points; four hidden layers at widths 20, 35, and 50.
evaluations.metric: Average test accuracy over the last 100 of 500 epochs and training time.
evaluations.result: ReLU versus NestNet accuracy is 0.738290/0.873631, 0.816048/0.995962, and 0.866118/0.999984; NestNet training is about 60% slower in each case.
evaluations.baseline: Same affine architecture with ordinary ReLU, but not matched for executed nonlinear operations.

evaluations.setting: Fashion-MNIST with a small two-convolutional-layer network; 18 runs, symmetrically trimmed to 12.
evaluations.metric: Best accuracy, mean of best 100 accuracies, last-100-epoch mean, and training time.
evaluations.result: Last-100 mean improves from 0.924447 to 0.926032 and best accuracy from 0.925290 to 0.926620; runtime rises from about 5,802 to 7,217 seconds.
evaluations.baseline: Same CNN using ReLU instead of the shared ten-parameter subnetwork at selected activations.

evaluations.setting: Theoretical approximation of continuous and alpha-Hölder functions on the d-dimensional unit cube.
evaluations.metric: Lp approximation error per distinct trainable-parameter budget.
evaluations.result: Constructive rate scales as omega_f(n^(-(s+1)/d)), or n^(-(s+1)alpha/d) for alpha-Hölder targets.
evaluations.baseline: The cited optimal n^(-2/d) distinct-parameter rate for standard ReLU networks under their conventional architecture class.

limitations: Parameter count omits repeated activation executions, expanded graph size, FLOPs, memory traffic, and communication, so it is not a complete efficiency measure.
Arbitrary-precision real weights and bit extraction are unpriced; finite precision, bounded weights, and perturbation robustness could erase the constructive rate.
The existence theorem gives no optimizer, sample complexity, statistical generalization, or guarantee that gradient training finds the constructed solution.
Only an upper bound is proved for NestNets; there is no matching lower bound or proof that the height-dependent rate is optimal or requires height.
The theory covers ReLU and continuous or Hölder target functions, not discontinuous targets, Sobolev error, robustness, or probabilistic learning.
The curse-of-dimensionality statement depends on height scaling with dimension and has dimension/height-dependent constants.
Only height-two models are trained, despite the asymptotic headline depending on arbitrary height s.
The synthetic spiral is exceptionally aligned with high-frequency piecewise-linear activations and has no matched-frequency-feature baseline.
Fashion-MNIST gains are small, trimmed after outcome ranking, and lack uncertainty or equal-runtime comparison.
The height-two experiment omits the algebraically matching 2019 VAF baseline and other learned-activation controls.
No modern image, language, scientific-learning, or high-dimensional regression benchmark is evaluated.
failure_modes: Deeply nested shared activations create long effective computation and unstable or highly correlated gradients.
Finite-precision perturbations corrupt densely encoded lookup values or narrow almost-step transitions.
A globally shared scalar activation is too restrictive when layers or channels need different nonlinearities.
Optimization collapses breakpoints or saturates the learned activation far from the proof construction.
Inference cost grows despite a small serialized parameter file because the same subnetwork is invoked at many sites.
The architecture overfits an oscillatory synthetic boundary but offers negligible gain on natural data.
Increasing height to match dimension becomes impractical before the theoretical exponent advantage appears.
reusable_insights: Report distinct parameters, expanded operations, activation calls, latency, memory, and numerical precision together for weight-shared architectures.
Treat learned activation functions as reusable modules and compare them against matched unshared, recurrent, spline, rational, and ordinary-depth controls.
Separate representational existence, stable finite-precision representation, trainability, and statistical learnability.
When a rate relies on bit encoding in real weights, add bounded-weight, quantized, and perturbation-stability analyses.
Use scaling experiments on controlled function families to test an approximation-rate theorem directly.
Match both parameter count and compute when claiming an architectural expressivity advantage.
open_questions: What approximation rate remains under bounded weights, b-bit quantization, and Lipschitz dependence on parameters?
How does NestNet compare with an exactly expanded weight-tied ReLU graph at matched FLOPs and latency?
Can higher-height NestNets be trained reliably, and how do gradient norms scale with height and reuse count?
Are there lower bounds for shared-weight computation that jointly account for distinct parameters and executed units?
Which tasks benefit from globally reused activation subnetworks rather than layer- or channel-specific ones?
Does the theoretical rate appear in regression experiments as n, height, dimension, and precision vary?
Can nesting be combined with sparse execution so that parameter efficiency translates into runtime efficiency?

competitive_landscape.title: A Simple and Efficient Architecture for Trainable Activation Functions
competitive_landscape.difference: The paper introduces the Variable Activation Function as a learned weighted sum of shifted and scaled base activations, and its k=3 ReLU form is algebraically the ten-parameter rho used in NestNet's height-two experiments. NestNet's defensible addition is arbitrary recursive height plus its distinct-parameter theorem, not this practical activation module.
competitive_landscape.source_version: arXiv primary record and full paper checked 2026-08-23

competitive_landscape.title: Learning Implicitly Recurrent CNNs Through Parameter Sharing
competitive_landscape.difference: Savarese and Maire learn combinations from a global filter-template bank and discover recurrent layer structure, explicitly evaluating parameter savings and extrapolation; NestNet instead shares scalar activation subnetworks recursively and proves a distinct-parameter approximation rate.

competitive_landscape.title: Rational Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Boulle et al. learn low-degree rational activation coefficients and prove efficient smooth-function approximation with practical PDE and GAN experiments; NestNet allows arbitrary ReLU subnetworks as activations and targets continuous/Hölder rates through recursive reuse.

competitive_landscape.title: Deep Neural Networks with ReLU-Sine-Exponential Activations Break Curse of Dimensionality in Approximation on Holder Class
competitive_landscape.difference: Jiao et al. obtain dimension-favorable Holder approximation using fixed ReLU, sine, and exponential activations at shallow depth; NestNet retains only ReLU primitives but gains rate through nested shared computation and arbitrary-precision lookup constructions.

competitive_landscape.title: KAN: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: KANs replace scalar edge weights with spline-parameterized univariate functions and emphasize interpretable fitting and scientific discovery; NestNet places shared ReLU subnetworks at nodes and emphasizes worst-case approximation per distinct parameter.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: Height is a third architectural dimension that makes ReLU NestNets substantially more expressive than width-depth networks, achieving n^(-(s+1)/d) Lipschitz approximation and escaping dimensionality when height is large enough.
novelty_assessment.evidence: A detailed recursive construction proves the distinct-parameter rate, and one shared ten-parameter activation yields large spiral gains and a small Fashion-MNIST gain over ReLU controls.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: Recursive activation subnetworks are a clear formalization of a useful weight-sharing pattern, and the theorem is technically substantial. The comparison is narrower than 'more expressive' suggests because a NestNet is an expanded ordinary ReLU graph with tied weights; the rate prices distinct coefficients while omitting execution and bit precision. The implemented height-two activation is an existing VAF form, and the empirical validation neither compares that antecedent nor tests the asymptotic theorem.

reviewer_notes: Read all 37 extracted pages, including the recursive definition, theorem constants, full construction and bit-extraction lemmas, experiment protocols, tables, and stated limitations. The audit distinguishes distinct-parameter expressivity from compute- or precision-matched efficiency and checks the dimensionality claim against height and finite-precision assumptions. It also notes a harmless sign typo for K in the page-six proof sketch (the theorem and appendix use the correct positive exponent) and that two supporting lemmas are imported from prior work. The exact VAF antecedent and primary parameter-sharing, approximation, trainable-activation, and subsequent KAN papers were checked on arXiv and NeurIPS proceedings on 2026-08-23.
